outcome: A September 2026 preprint by Taylor Gordon claims an explicit construction of universal point sets for general planar graphs of size n^{1+o(1)} (n·exp(O(sqrt(log n)))), improving the quadratic upper bound that had stood as the state of the art through the 2025 Dujmović–Morin survey and through the frozen Wikipedia revision. This is not yet an expert-digested resolution: the preprint is 12 days old, has a single arXiv version, no journal reference, and the only secondary commentary found treats it explicitly as unverified.

ai.basis_quote: This paper was prepared with substantial assistance from GPT-6 Astra. Starting from the author's interval-based approach, the model helped develop the construction, formulate and revise the proof, check finite examples, and draft the exposition.

summary: Wikipedia's frozen January 2024 revision states that closing the gap between the linear lower bound and quadratic upper bound for universal point sets of general planar graphs is open, and the general (unrestricted) case remained quadratic as of the 2025 Dujmović–Morin survey 'Free Sets in Planar Graphs: History and Applications' (arXiv:2403.17090), confirming nothing changed between the frozen date and late 2025. On 10 September 2026, Taylor Gordon posted arXiv:2609.10916, 'Almost Linear Universal Point Sets for Planar Graphs,' claiming an explicit construction of size n^{1+o(1)} via a reduction to superpatterns for 213-avoiding permutations (building on the Bannister–Cheng–Devanny–Eppstein reduction), represented through ordered rooted forests and layered intervals. The abstract and conclusion both explicitly credit GPT-6 Astra with assisting in developing the construction and the proof itself ('the model helped develop the construction, formulate and revise the proof, check finite examples, and draft the exposition') — this is authors'-own-account language describing the model contributing to the mathematics, not merely checking or formalizing human-produced work, so ai_role is coded 'assisted' rather than 'generated' (a human, Gordon, is credited as directing/producing the result with substantial AI help) or 'none'. The paper includes a Lean 4 formalization, but by the authors' own statement this formalization covers only 'an earlier construction' and explicitly does NOT cover 'the layered proof presented here' — so the Lean check does not certify the actual theorem as stated. No expert digestion, journal acceptance, or independent verification of this specific result was found. The one piece of secondary commentary located, an article on llmrumors.com surveying September 2026 GPT-6-Astra-credited arXiv papers, explicitly discusses this paper and cautions that 'a model name cannot carry a theorem,' that arXiv moderation is not peer review, and that the linked Lean code covers the earlier construction, not the new near-linear result — i.e., it treats the paper as an unverified claim, not a resolution. No retraction, refutation, or identified flaw was found either. Given all this — a very recent single-version preprint, explicit disclosure that the formal verification does not cover the claimed result, and no expert working through the argument — this is coded 'claimed,' not 'resolved.' The direction is 'confirmed' because the claimed result, if correct, answers the open question in the direction of existence of a subquadratic (indeed near-linear) universal point set, matching what was conjectured/hoped rather than refuting it; there is no counterexample involved.
competing_reading: One could argue this should be 'progress' rather than 'claimed', on the theory that an unverified single-author preprint with heavy but partial AI assistance and an admittedly incomplete formalization is closer to an unconfirmed rumor than a checkable claim. I coded 'claimed' because the preprint does present an explicit, fully written construction and proof (not just a bound-improvement sketch), which is what distinguishes 'claimed' from 'progress' in §6.1 — but confidence that this preprint will hold up under scrutiny is low given the total absence of independent human review at the time of writing, and given that other GPT-6 Astra proof attempts surveyed in the same news piece (Quang Hung Tran's geometry conjectures) turned out to be incomplete.
what_would_settle_it: Either (a) an expert in graph drawing (e.g. Dujmović, Morin, Eppstein, or another author in this specific subfield) publishing a review, a conference/journal acceptance, or a blog post working through Gordon's construction and confirming or refuting the n^{1+o(1)} bound, or (b) a full Lean/Coq formalization of the actual layered-interval proof (not just 'an earlier construction') that compiles without `sorry`, or (c) a follow-up preprint identifying a gap or counterexample to the construction.

judgement.doubts: Scope call: JUDGE.md F3 cites universal point sets as an example where n^{1+o(1)} does not close a linear-versus-quadratic gap. But this bullet's wording asks only for universal point sets of subquadratic size, and n^{1+o(1)} is subquadratic, so against the bullet's own words the claim is whole. If the question is instead read as the gap between linear and quadratic (as Wikipedia's article phrases it), the scope becomes bound and the status becomes progress. AI role is assisted: the model helped develop the construction and proof, which is mathematics in the result, not just checking. The Lean build does not cover the claimed theorem (F10). I did not read the Pith Review page, and it is not verification anyway (F11).
